sections.minutes: sum of the subsection time boxes (61)
sections.order_note: Teaching order follows one event: it runs in an execution environment (1), reaches the function by push or by polling (2), fails and is retried by the caller or by Lambda (3), or arrives in a batch from a queue or a stream (4); then capacity: the shared Regional quota (5), reserved concurrency (6), provisioned concurrency (7) and memory with its CPU (8); then the code (9), the permissions (10), the network (11), the database (12), the HTTP front door (13) and the compute choice with its price (14). sections.heading: Each request runs in an execution environment that Lambda can freeze and reuse

plan.problem: A team moves a small job from its server into a function. The old code kept a cache in memory and wrote temporary files to disk. Which of these still works?
trace: **Create.** When no environment is free, Lambda [downloads your code, starts the environment] (lambda-cold-start-definition) and runs the [Init phase] (lambda-lifecycle-phases): extensions and the runtime start, and the static code outside the handler runs.

**Invoke.** Lambda [sends an Invoke event to the runtime] (lambda-lifecycle-phases), and the handler, the [method in your function code that processes events] (lambda-function-single-handler), runs; the timeout [limits the duration of the entire Invoke phase] (lambda-invoke-phase-limited-by-timeout).

**Freeze and reuse.** Afterwards [the execution environment is frozen]; for the next request [Lambda can reuse the environment], a [warm start] (lambda-warm-start-environment-reuse), and the Init code [is not run again] (lambda-static-init-reuse-connections).
**Recycle.** Lambda [terminates execution environments every few hours] (lambda-environment-not-persistent), even for a function that is busy all the time.
plan.table: What survives (columns: Kept in | Next warm invocation | A new environment): a variable set in Init code | yes: it [is not run again] (lambda-static-init-reuse-connections) | no; a file in /tmp | yes: it [remains when the execution environment is frozen] (lambda-tmp-transient-cache) | no: /tmp is [temporary and unique to each execution environment] (lambda-tmp-unique-per-environment); an item in DynamoDB or an object in Amazon S3 | yes | yes: a [durable store such as Amazon S3] (lambda-stateless-store-state-elsewhere).
plan.why: Why stateless? An environment serves [a maximum of one invocation at a time] (lambda-managed-instances-multi-concurrency-row), so Lambda scales by adding environments, and each one has its own memory and disk; AWS says a function [exists only for a single invocation] in its design (lambda-stateless-store-state-elsewhere). Keep the second link only if it is not used in the table.
plan.exam_signal: "reuse the database connection between invocations" points to code in the initialization phase, outside the handler (lambda-static-init-reuse-connections); "keep user sessions between requests" points to a durable store such as DynamoDB, not the function (lambda-stateless-store-state-elsewhere).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: each request gets an environment, and Lambda reuses warm ones. The thing to watch is that nothing in the environment lasts.
plan.stop_and_answer: A function counts orders in a global variable and returns the total. Two requests arrive at the same moment after a quiet minute. Do both responses show the same total? Answer: not necessarily; requests can be [processed out of order or concurrently] (lambda-requests-out-of-order), and concurrent requests run in different environments with their own counters. Store the count in DynamoDB. Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: AWS services push events to a function and Lambda polls queues and streams
sections.diagram: lambda-invocation-paths, after the table (its alt and caption count toward this subsection: keep the alt at about 40 words)

plan.problem: An upload, a message in a queue and a nightly schedule should each start work. In each case, something must tell the function that there is work.
trace: **Push.** In [direct invocation (push)] a service invokes the function (lambda-event-push-or-pull): Amazon S3 is [Event-driven; asynchronous invocation] (lambda-trigger-s3-async), and Amazon API Gateway is [Event-driven; synchronous invocation] (lambda-trigger-apigateway-sync).

**Pull.** Queues and streams use [event source mappings (pull)] (lambda-event-push-or-pull): [Lambda handles the polling] (lambda-esm-lambda-polls-source), and the mapping can [batch records together] (lambda-esm-batches-records).

**Where the setting lives.** A trigger is [stored and managed by the service] that creates the events; an event source mapping is [created and managed within the Lambda service] (lambda-trigger-stored-by-source-esm-in-lambda).
plan.table: How each source starts the function (columns: Source | Push or pull | Invocation): Amazon S3, Amazon SNS | push | asynchronous (lambda-trigger-s3-async, lambda-trigger-sns-async); Amazon EventBridge rules, EventBridge Scheduler | push | [asynchronous invocation (event buses and rules)] (lambda-trigger-eventbridge-async-rules), [Event-driven (time based); asynchronous invocation] (lambda-trigger-scheduler-async); API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, Amazon Cognito | push | synchronous (lambda-trigger-apigateway-sync, lambda-trigger-alb-sync, lambda-trigger-cognito-sync); Amazon SQS, Amazon Kinesis, DynamoDB streams | pull | [Event source mapping] (lambda-trigger-sqs-esm, lambda-trigger-kinesis-esm, lambda-trigger-dynamodb-esm). Each cell without a link holds no number and no absolute word.
plan.why: Why does Lambda poll queues? A queue never sends anything by itself: Amazon SQS is [Pull-based (consumers poll messages from the queue)] (lambda-trigger-sqs-sns-eventbridge-model), so Lambda runs the consumer for you, and you write no polling code.
plan.exam_signal: "process each new object as soon as it is uploaded" points to an S3 event notification that invokes a function (lambda-trigger-s3-async); "an instance checks the bucket every minute for new files" is the pattern to replace: [Polling can be highly inefficient] (lambda-eda-polling-inefficient).
plan.body_extras: One sentence after the Exam signal: one function that calls another and waits is [generally an anti-pattern] (lambda-chaining-anti-pattern-sqs-or-step-functions), because the caller keeps [running in a wait state] and is billed for it (lambda-chaining-cost-wait-state); put an SQS queue or AWS Step Functions between them (chapter 32, xref marker).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: services push events to the function, and Lambda pulls from queues and streams. The thing to watch is which side owns the setting.
plan.stop_and_answer: An S3 bucket and an SQS queue both start the same function. Can one invocation receive records from the bucket and the queue together? Answer: no; a function [can have multiple triggers], but each event [has data from only one trigger] (lambda-multiple-triggers-one-per-event). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: A synchronous caller handles errors itself but Lambda retries asynchronous events

plan.problem: An order function fails once in a while. Whether a failed order is lost depends on how the function was invoked, not on the code.
trace: **Synchronous.** Lambda [runs the function and waits for a response] (lambda-sync-invocation-waits). On an error the caller can [view the error message in the response] and must [retry the invocation manually] (lambda-sync-error-caller-retries); the AWS CLI and SDKs [automatically retry on client timeouts] (lambda-sdk-cli-auto-retry).
**Asynchronous.** Lambda [places the event in a queue] and [returns a success response] at once; [A separate process reads events from the queue] (lambda-async-queue-then-separate-process).
**Retry.** After a function error Lambda tries [two more times] (lambda-async-default-two-retries); throttled events are retried for [up to 6 hours by default] (lambda-async-throttle-retry-6-hours).
**Keep or lose.** When the retries end, [Lambda discards it], unless you [configure a failed-event destination] (lambda-async-discard-then-destination).
plan.table: Who does what (columns: Question | Synchronous | Asynchronous): who waits | the caller (lambda-sync-invocation-waits) | nobody: Lambda [returns a success response] (lambda-async-queue-then-separate-process); who retries | the caller (lambda-sync-error-caller-retries) | Lambda, [two more times] (lambda-async-default-two-retries); largest request payload | [6 MB] (lambda-payload-sync) | [1 MB] (lambda-payload-async); where a failed event ends | in the caller's error handling | discarded, or in a destination (lambda-async-discard-then-destination).
plan.why: Why does Lambda not retry a synchronous call? The caller is still waiting for the answer, and for a synchronous call by a service [The service controls the error strategy] (lambda-sync-service-controls-error-strategy).
plan.exam_signal: "no failed event from the upload trigger can be lost" points to an on-failure destination such as [A standard SQS queue] (lambda-async-destination-targets); "the client must see the error at once" points to a synchronous call: API Gateway [always relays the error response back] (lambda-apigateway-relays-error).
plan.try_it: Try it callout for lambda-t03 after the table, ending with its task comment.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: destinations or a dead-letter queue. A destination can be [A standard SQS queue], [A standard SNS topic], [A Lambda function], [An EventBridge event bus] or [An Amazon S3 bucket (on failure only)] (lambda-async-destination-targets); a FIFO queue or topic is an [unsupported destination type] (lambda-destination-fifo-unsupported). A dead-letter queue [only sends the content of the event] (lambda-dlq-content-only-vs-destinations), without the error details. You can set the retries [between 0 and 2] (lambda-async-retry-attempts-0-to-2) and the event age [up to 6 hours] (lambda-async-max-event-age-6-hours). At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: in a synchronous call the caller retries, and in an asynchronous call Lambda retries. The thing to watch is where a failed event goes.
plan.stop_and_answer: A function that Amazon S3 invokes never fails, yet some results are written twice. How can that happen? Answer: [the queue itself is eventually consistent] (lambda-async-queue-eventually-consistent), so the function can receive the same event more than once; make it idempotent (lambda-idempotent-functions). Keep these facts out of the trace.

sections.heading: A failed batch returns to its queue but blocks its stream shard

plan.problem: A function reads orders from a queue and events from a stream. One record makes the function fail every time. What happens to all the other records?
trace: **Batch.** The mapping invokes the function when [The batch size is met], when [The batching window reaches its maximum value], or when the payload reaches [6 MB] (lambda-esm-batch-triggers-three-criteria); for SQS the default batch size is [10] (lambda-sqs-batch-size).

**Queue failure.** The messages of a batch stay hidden for the visibility timeout; after an error they [become visible in the queue again] (lambda-sqs-visibility-timeout-retry). The queue's own [visibility timeout and redrive policy] decide when they are retried and where failed messages go (lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue).

**Stream failure.** Lambda processes each shard in order and [stops processing additional records in a shard] after an error (lambda-kinesis-in-order-stops-on-error); stream records are retried until the function [succeeds or the data expires] (lambda-faq-streams-retry-until-expiry).
**Duplicates.** Event source mappings [process each event at least once] (lambda-esm-at-least-once), so the code must be idempotent (lambda-idempotent-functions).
plan.table: Queue or stream (columns: Question | SQS queue | Kinesis or DynamoDB stream): after an error | the messages [become visible in the queue again] (lambda-sqs-visibility-timeout-retry) | the mapping [pauses processing for the affected shard] (lambda-esm-stream-reprocess-batch-pause-shard); where failed records end | the source queue's dead-letter queue: SQS can [send it to a dead-letter queue] (lambda-sqs-dlq-maxreceivecount-5) | an on-failure destination such as an [Amazon SNS topic, Amazon SQS queue] (lambda-kinesis-on-failure-destination-targets); retry only the failed part | a [partial batch response] (lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response) | bisect: it [splits a failed batch into two smaller batches] (lambda-stream-bisect-batch-on-error).
plan.why: Why does a stream wait? A stream keeps the order of the records in a shard, so Lambda [reprocesses the entire batch] and holds the shard (lambda-esm-stream-reprocess-batch-pause-shard); a queue makes no such promise, so the other messages keep moving.
plan.exam_signal: "messages that fail again and again must be kept for analysis" with an SQS trigger points to a dead-letter queue in the source queue's redrive policy, with a maxReceiveCount of [at least 5] (lambda-sqs-dlq-maxreceivecount-5); "one bad record stops processing of the stream for days" points to bisect, a retry limit and an on-failure destination: by default a bad record can block a shard for [up to one week] (lambda-kinesis-bad-record-block-one-week).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug (one of the two in the file): a function has a timeout of 5 minutes, and its SQS queue keeps the default visibility timeout of 30 seconds. The team creates the event source mapping. (The prompt numbers are example values.) Reveal: the function timeout [must be less than or equal to] the visibility timeout, and Lambda [returns an error] when it is not (lambda-sqs-timeout-not-above-visibility); AWS recommends a visibility timeout of [at least six times] the function timeout (lambda-sqs-visibility-six-times-timeout). Place it after the Exam trap and before the Go deeper; about 60 words with its reveal.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: SQS scaling. For a standard queue Lambda starts with [five batches at a time with five concurrent invocations], adds [up to 300 more concurrent invokes per minute], and one mapping reaches [1,250] concurrent invokes (lambda-sqs-scaling-5-batches-300-per-minute-1250); provisioned mode reaches [up to 100,000 concurrent function invocations] (lambda-sqs-esm-1250-default-100000-provisioned). Maximum concurrency, [between 2 and 1,000] (lambda-sqs-max-concurrency-range), caps one source. A record that matches no filter is dropped: [Lambda discards the record] (lambda-filter-five-ored-discard). At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a failed queue batch comes back later, and a failed stream batch holds its shard. The thing to watch is the visibility timeout.
plan.stop_and_answer: A Kinesis stream has 100 shards, and the function falls behind. The team cannot add shards. Which setting lets more batches run at once? Answer: the parallelization factor, [from 1 (default) to 10] concurrent batches per shard (lambda-kinesis-parallelization-factor-1-to-10). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: One Regional concurrency quota is shared by all functions and throttles the excess

plan.problem: A marketing email brings ten times the usual traffic. The functions scale, and then some requests fail. Which limit did they reach?
trace: **Count.** Concurrency is estimated by [Multiplying average requests per second] by the average duration in seconds (lambda-concurrency-formula): at half a second per request, a load of 100 requests per second needs [50 instances of your function to handle a load of 100 requests per second] (lambda-concurrency-example-100-rps-500-ms).

**Share.** The functions of one account in one Region share one quota: [1,000] by default, adjustable to [Tens of thousands] (lambda-concurrent-executions-default) through [Service Quotas] (lambda-faq-limit-increase-service-quotas).

**Scale.** Each function scales on its own (a [function-level limit], lambda-faq-scaling-limit-per-function), by [1,000 additional execution environment instances] every 10 seconds (lambda-scaling-rate-10000-rps).
**Throttle.** Requests beyond that fail with a [throttling error (429 status code)] (lambda-throttle-429).
plan.table: What a throttle does to each caller (columns: Invoked by | The caller sees | What happens next): API Gateway or an SDK call | a [429 error code] (lambda-faq-throttle-sync-429) | the caller retries; the SDKs [automatically retry on client timeouts] (lambda-sdk-cli-auto-retry); Amazon S3 or Amazon SNS | a success response | Lambda retries for [up to 6 hours by default] (lambda-async-throttle-retry-6-hours); an SQS event source mapping | nothing | [Lambda continues to retry the message] until the visibility timeout ends (lambda-sqs-throttle-drop-after-visibility).
plan.why: Why one shared pool? The quota is a [default safety throttle] (lambda-faq-parallel-no-limit-safety-throttle) for the whole account, so one runaway function hits a ceiling before it hits your bill; reserved concurrency (next subsection) divides the pool.
plan.exam_signal: "the functions return TooManyRequestsException during a campaign" points to a concurrency quota increase in [Service Quotas] (lambda-faq-limit-increase-service-quotas); "the standby Region must take the full load after a failover" points to the same increase in the standby Region ahead of time, because the quotas apply [per AWS Region] (lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: all functions in a Region share one concurrency quota. The thing to watch is the standby Region, which has a quota of its own.
plan.stop_and_answer: A function was quiet for an hour, so it 'saved up' scaling. Can it now add three times the usual number of environments in one step? Answer: no; unused scaling capacity does not accumulate: the rate is [always 1,000 concurrency units at maximum] (lambda-scaling-rate-not-accrued). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: Reserved concurrency guarantees and caps the concurrency of one function at no charge

plan.problem: A nightly batch function takes the whole account pool, and the payment function is throttled. In another team, a small database fails when too many copies of a function connect at once.
trace: **Reserve.** Reserved concurrency can [reserve a subset of your account concurrency limit] for a critical function, or [cap traffic rates to downstream resources] (lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control).
**Cap.** The same number is the function's ceiling: it can [limit how high your function can scale] (lambda-bp-reserved-protects-downstream).

**Keep a floor for the rest.** Lambda keeps [100 units of concurrency] for functions without a reservation (lambda-unreserved-concurrency-100-always), so at the default quota you can reserve [up to 900 units of concurrency] (lambda-reserve-up-to-900-default).
**Stop.** To stop a function, [set its reserved concurrency to 0] (lambda-reserved-concurrency-zero-throttles).
plan.table: One setting, three uses (columns: Goal | Set | Effect): a critical function must always scale | reserved concurrency on that function | its share is kept: [reserve a subset of your account concurrency limit] (lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control); a database must not be overwhelmed | reserved concurrency on the caller | [limit how high your function can scale] (lambda-bp-reserved-protects-downstream); a runaway function must stop now | reserved concurrency 0 | [throttle all invocations to the function] (lambda-bp-runaway-reserved-zero).
plan.why: Why is it free? A reservation only divides the pool you already have and creates nothing: configuring it [incurs no additional charges] (lambda-reserved-concurrency-no-charge).
plan.exam_signal: "one critical function must keep capacity when other functions are busy" points to reserved concurrency on that function (lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control); "stop a function immediately without deleting it" points to reserved concurrency 0 (lambda-bp-runaway-reserved-zero).
plan.try_it: Try it callout for lambda-t02 after the table, ending with its task comment.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: recursive loops. A function that writes to the bucket or queue that invokes it can loop, and a loop can [use all of your account's available concurrency] (lambda-recursion-unintended-cost-concurrency). Recursive loop detection is [turned on by default for all AWS customers] (lambda-recursion-on-by-default-free) and stops a chain after [approximately 16 times] (lambda-recursion-stops-about-16), for loops through [Amazon SQS, Amazon S3, Amazon SNS] (lambda-recursion-supported-services). For a loop that it does not detect, reserved concurrency 0 stops the function. At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: reserved concurrency sets aside part of the pool for one function and caps it there. The thing to watch is that it warms nothing.
plan.stop_and_answer: An asynchronously invoked function has a dead-letter queue. During an incident the team sets its reserved concurrency to 0. What happens to new events? Answer: Lambda sends them to the dead-letter queue or on-failure destination [without any retries] (lambda-reserved-zero-async-to-dlq-no-retry). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized and you pay for them while idle

plan.problem: A mobile app's API answers fast during the day, but after a quiet period the first requests take seconds, and customers notice.
trace: **Prepare.** Provisioned concurrency is a number of [pre-initialized execution environments] (lambda-pc-scales-beyond-setting) that are ready to respond in [double-digit milliseconds] (lambda-faq-pc-what).

**Point at a version.** It applies to [a specific version or alias of a function], [not the $LATEST version] (lambda-pc-not-latest-no-cold-start); the event source must call that alias, the one that [points to the correct function alias or version] (lambda-pc-event-source-alias).

**Overflow.** Beyond the setting, Lambda scales [above and beyond your provisioned concurrency setting] with on-demand environments (lambda-pc-scales-beyond-setting), which can have cold starts and are [billed for excess function execution] at the on-demand rate (lambda-pc-excess-at-on-demand-rate).

**Pay.** You pay for the [amount of concurrency you configure] and for how long (lambda-pc-pricing-dimensions), [rounded up to the nearest five minutes] (lambda-pc-rounded-5-minutes), even with no requests: [it increases costs] (lambda-pc-costs-while-idle).
plan.table: Three settings that sound alike (columns: Setting | First requests | Extra charge): provisioned concurrency | fast: it [does not exhibit cold start behavior] (lambda-pc-not-latest-no-cold-start) | yes, while configured (lambda-pc-pricing-dimensions); SnapStart | faster, [as low as sub-second] (lambda-snapstart-vs-pc-guide) | caching and restore (lambda-faq-snapstart-pricing); reserved concurrency | unchanged | none: it [incurs no additional charges] (lambda-reserved-concurrency-no-charge).
plan.why: Why pay while nothing happens? The environments are initialized and wait for you all the time, and for these functions the [free tier does not apply] (lambda-pc-no-free-tier).
plan.exam_signal: "traffic rises at the same time every morning, and the API must stay fast" points to provisioned concurrency that [Application Auto Scaling] adjusts on a schedule (lambda-faq-pc-application-auto-scaling); "strict double-digit millisecond startup" points to provisioned concurrency, because SnapStart is a [best-effort optimization] (lambda-faq-snapstart-vs-pc).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: SnapStart. SnapStart resumes from a [pre-initialized snapshot] (lambda-faq-snapstart-how), for [Java 11 and later], [Python 3.12 and later] and [.NET 8 and later] (lambda-snapstart-runtimes-guide), and [only on published function versions] (lambda-snapstart-published-versions-only). It [cannot be enabled at the same time] as provisioned concurrency (lambda-faq-snapstart-pc-exclusive), and it does not work with Amazon EFS or [ephemeral storage greater than 512 MB] (lambda-snapstart-unsupported-features). At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: provisioned concurrency keeps environments ready, so the first requests are fast. The thing to watch is that you pay for them all day.
plan.stop_and_answer: A function has a reserved concurrency of 50. The team tries to configure a provisioned concurrency of 80. Does Lambda accept it? Answer: no; you [can't allocate more provisioned concurrency than reserved concurrency] (lambda-provisioned-not-above-reserved). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: Memory is the one size setting and CPU grows in proportion to it

plan.problem: An image function is slow because its code calculates a lot. The team looks for a CPU setting in the console and does not find one.
trace: **Choose memory.** Memory is set between [128 MB] and [10,240 MB] in [1-MB increments] (lambda-memory-range); the default, [128 MB], is the lowest setting (lambda-memory-default).

**Get CPU with it.** Lambda allocates CPU [in proportion to the amount of memory] (lambda-cpu-proportional-to-memory); at [1,769 MB] a function has the equivalent of [one vCPU] (lambda-one-vcpu-at-1769-mb).
**Set the timeout.** The timeout starts at [3 seconds] and can be raised to [900 seconds (15 minutes)] (lambda-timeout-default).
**Add disk if needed.** The /tmp directory holds [between 512 MB and 10,240 MB] (lambda-tmp-transient-cache).
plan.table: Which setting fixes which problem (columns: Problem | Raise | Fact): CPU-bound or network-bound code | memory | [increasing the memory can help resolve the compute] bottleneck (lambda-memory-tuning-cpu-bound); a run longer than the timeout | the timeout, up to [900 seconds] (lambda-timeout-max) | ; large temporary files | /tmp storage, up to [10,240 MB] (lambda-tmp-storage-range) |. Merge the second and third columns if the table runs long.
plan.why: Why one setting? You choose the memory, and Lambda allocates [proportional CPU power] (lambda-faq-memory-cpu-proportional). Duration is billed [measured in GB-seconds] (lambda-pricing-dimensions), so each millisecond costs more at a larger size, and a faster run can offset it. No verified fact says that the cost stays flat or falls (brief.v0 d034): write it as a trade-off to measure, never as a promise.
plan.exam_signal: "choose the memory size from measured data" points to the [AWS Lambda Power Tuning project] (lambda-right-size-memory-power-tuning) or to Compute Optimizer, which [supports only functions that use x86_64 architecture] (lambda-compute-optimizer-x86-only).
plan.body_extras: One sentence, only if words remain: functions on arm64 can get [significantly better price and performance] (lambda-arm64-better-price-performance). No percentage: no saved AWS page states one (brief.v0 d087).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: raise the memory, and the CPU rises with it. The thing to watch is the price of each millisecond.
plan.stop_and_answer: A calculation needs eight vCPUs working in parallel. Which memory setting gives a function that much CPU? Answer: none; CPU scales with memory [up to 6 vCPU] (lambda-cpu-up-to-6-vcpu), while Fargate offers [0.25 vCPUs to 32 vCPUs] (lambda-vs-fargate-cpu-memory-ceilings). Keep these facts out of the trace.

sections.heading: Code ships as a zip archive or an image and published versions never change

plan.problem: A function needs a large machine learning library, and the team wants each release to reach a small share of users first.
trace: **Package.** A function is deployed as [.zip file archives] or [container images] (lambda-faq-deploy-zip-or-image). A .zip archive is [50 MB] zipped for a direct upload (lambda-zip-package-50-mb) and [250 MB] unzipped with its layers (lambda-package-250-mb-unzipped); an image can be [10 GB] (lambda-container-image-10-gb), from Amazon ECR [in the same AWS Region] (lambda-container-image-ecr-same-region).

**Share code.** A layer is a [.zip file archive that contains supplementary code] (lambda-layer-zip-contents); a function uses [up to five layers] (lambda-layers-five-and-250-mb), and you can [use layers only with Lambda functions] deployed as .zip archives (lambda-layers-zip-only).

**Publish.** A published version is [immutable]; the version you edit is the [unpublished version is named $LATEST] (lambda-version-immutable-latest-unpublished). Rephrase around the display if it reads badly, keeping it verbatim.

**Point and shift.** An alias is [a pointer to a function version] (lambda-alias-pointer-to-version); a weighted alias sends a [small percentage of traffic] to the new version, so you can [quickly roll back] (lambda-weighted-alias-canary).
plan.table: Which package (columns: Need | Package | Size): small code with common libraries | .zip archive | [250 MB] unzipped (lambda-package-250-mb-unzipped); large libraries or your own base image | container image | [10 GB] (lambda-container-image-10-gb); libraries shared by several functions | a layer | [up to five layers] per function (lambda-layers-five-and-250-mb).
plan.why: Why immutable versions? A release is undone by moving the alias back, and settings that need a fixed version, such as provisioned concurrency, attach to [a specific version or alias of a function] (lambda-pc-not-latest-no-cold-start).
plan.exam_signal: "send a small share of traffic to the new version and roll back fast" points to a weighted alias (lambda-weighted-alias-canary); "the dependencies are larger than the deployment package quota" points to a container image (lambda-container-image-10-gb).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: with managed runtimes Lambda can [apply these updates automatically] for security patches, but for a container image [you're responsible for rebuilding your function's container image] (lambda-runtime-patching-managed-vs-image); a .zip archive on a managed runtime is the lower-overhead choice when both fit.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: ship large code as an image, and release with versions and an alias. The thing to watch is $LATEST, which is the only version you edit.
plan.stop_and_answer: For quick tests, a team wants a weighted alias that sends 5 percent of traffic to $LATEST. Can it? Answer: no; a weighted alias [cannot point to $LATEST], and [Both versions must be published] (lambda-weighted-alias-two-versions-not-latest). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: An execution role grants permissions and a resource-based policy allows invocation

plan.problem: An upload must start a function, and the function must read the uploaded object and send a message to a queue. Two different policies decide these calls.
trace: **Outbound: the execution role.** Every function [must have an execution role] (lambda-execution-role-required-logs); [Lambda automatically assumes your execution role] when the function runs, and the role's trust policy names [lambda.amazonaws.com] (lambda-execution-role-trust-lambda-principal).

**Minimum.** The role needs CloudWatch Logs access, which [AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole] gives (lambda-execution-role-required-logs); then add what the code calls and [limit the execution role to these permissions] (lambda-bp-least-privilege-role).

**Inbound: the resource-based policy.** It can [grant other AWS accounts, users, organizations] and AWS services access to the function (lambda-resource-policy-grants-accounts-services); when Amazon S3 calls the function, [Lambda considers only the resource-based policy] (lambda-service-caller-resource-policy-only).
**Polling.** For an event source mapping the role decides: a role that [doesn't allow reading messages from the queue] is a configuration error (lambda-sqs-execution-role-read-permissions).
plan.table: Which policy decides (columns: Call | Decided by | Example): the function calls Amazon S3 or Amazon SQS | the execution role, an [IAM role] (lambda-faq-execution-role) | read the uploaded object; Amazon S3, Amazon SNS or another account invokes the function | the resource-based policy (lambda-service-caller-resource-policy-only) | an upload starts the function; Lambda polls a stream or queue for the function | the [Lambda function role] (lambda-faq-poll-controlled-by-role) | the uploads queue.
plan.why: Why two policies? The function acts as its role, but it is also a resource that others call. One large function with every permission makes least privilege [Hard to enforce least privilege] (lambda-monolith-breaks-least-privilege); one function for [a single, well-defined task] keeps each role small.
plan.exam_signal: "the function needs database credentials" points to AWS Secrets Manager: AWS says to [use AWS Secrets Manager instead of environment variables] (lambda-secrets-manager-not-env-vars); "a function in another account must be invoked" points to [add a cross-account permissions statement] to the function's policy (lambda-cross-account-resource-policy).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug (the second of the file): a team adds an S3 event notification to a bucket with the AWS CLI. The function's execution role allows s3:GetObject on the bucket. Uploads arrive, but the function never runs. Reveal: the execution role does not decide who may invoke; in the console [Lambda automatically adds the required permissions] to the resource-based policy (lambda-console-trigger-adds-resource-policy), but here nobody added a statement that lets s3.amazonaws.com invoke the function for this bucket. Place it after the Exam signal; about 60 words with its reveal.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the role says what the function can do, and the resource policy says who can call it. The thing to watch is S3, which needs the resource policy.
plan.stop_and_answer: A function's execution role has every S3 action on every bucket, but the code only reads one bucket. What should change before production? Answer: the role should [include only the required permissions] (lambda-exec-role-least-privilege): read access to that one bucket. Keep this fact out of the trace. Do not teach put-resource-policy or full IAM resource-based policies for functions: that change is not examinable yet (lambda-change-full-iam-resource-policies-2026).

sections.heading: A VPC function reaches private resources and needs a NAT gateway for the internet

plan.problem: A function must query a database in private subnets and also call a payment provider on the internet.
trace: **Default.** Every function runs in a VPC [owned and managed by the Lambda service] (lambda-runs-in-lambda-managed-vpc), and by default functions [have access to the public internet] (lambda-vpc-attached-only-vpc-resources).

**Attach.** To reach your resources you choose a [subnet and security group] (lambda-faq-vpc-subnet-security-group); [Lambda creates a Hyperplane ENI] for each [same subnet and security group combination] (lambda-hyperplane-eni-shared-by-subnet-sg), and the role needs permissions such as [AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole] (lambda-vpc-execution-role-policy).
**Lose the internet.** Once attached, the function [can only access resources available within that VPC] (lambda-vpc-attached-only-vpc-resources).

**Route out.** A public subnet [doesn't give it internet access]; use private subnets that [access the internet through the NAT gateway] (lambda-vpc-public-subnet-no-internet). Teach the NAT gateway route, never 'an internet gateway' for the function (register-18 note).
plan.table: What the function can reach (columns: Configuration | Private database | Internet API): not attached to a VPC | no | yes: [have access to the public internet] (lambda-vpc-attached-only-vpc-resources); attached to a public subnet | yes | no: it [doesn't give it internet access] (lambda-vpc-public-subnet-no-internet); attached to private subnets with a route to a NAT gateway | yes | yes: they [access the internet through the NAT gateway] (lambda-vpc-public-subnet-no-internet).
plan.why: Why does a public subnet not help? The function gets no public IP address from it; the route through a NAT gateway gives the private subnet its way out. The Serverless Lens says to configure VPC access [only when necessary] (lambda-wa-vpc-only-when-necessary).
plan.exam_signal: "clients in a VPC must invoke the function without internet access" points to an [interface VPC endpoint] for Lambda (lambda-interface-endpoint-private-invoke); "the function must read a database in private subnets" points to [attaching your function to the VPC] (lambda-vpc-attach-private-subnets).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: network interfaces and shared files. A VPC holds [3,000] Lambda network interfaces by default (lambda-eni-per-vpc-quota), a quota per VPC, not per Region (lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc); each supports [65,000 connections/ports] (lambda-hyperplane-eni-65000-connections). A new VPC function [remains in the Pending state] until its interface is ready (lambda-vpc-new-function-pending). For shared files, a function can [mount an Amazon Elastic File System] [over the local network in a VPC] (lambda-efs-shared-mount-in-vpc), with [a mount target in every Availability Zone] (lambda-efs-mount-target-every-az). At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: attach the function to private subnets and send internet traffic through a NAT gateway. The thing to watch is that a public subnet does not help.
plan.stop_and_answer: A VPC function was not invoked for three weeks. The next call fails, and the function shows Pending. What happened? Answer: after it was [idle for 14 days], Lambda reclaimed its network interfaces and set it to Inactive (lambda-vpc-idle-14-days-inactive). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: RDS Proxy pools the database connections that many concurrent functions would exhaust

plan.problem: On a busy day, many copies of a function each open their own connection to a PostgreSQL database, and the database stops accepting connections.
trace: **Scale out.** Lambda scales by creating many environments, and each keeps its own connection, so high concurrency can [exhaust database connection limits] (lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy).
**Fixed database.** Amazon RDS has fixed capacity, so [you might exceed your connection quota] (lambda-rds-connection-quota-spikes).

**Pool.** RDS Proxy lets applications [pool and share database connections] (rds-proxy-definition-pool-share); functions benefit from the [connection pooling offered by RDS Proxy] (rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling), and in a surge the proxy [queues or throttles application connections] (rds-proxy-surges-queue-throttle).
**Reuse.** Open the connection in the Init code, so that warm invocations [reuse connections over multiple invocations] (lambda-static-init-reuse-connections).
plan.table: Three ways to store the data (columns: Option | Connections | Fits): direct connections | one or more in each environment | simple scenarios; [proxies are recommended for production] (lambda-rds-proxy-recommended-production); RDS Proxy | pooled and shared (rds-proxy-definition-pool-share) | production traffic with spikes; DynamoDB | none: [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API] (lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections) | data that [don't require complex joins or transactions] (lambda-ddb-recommended-for-serverless).
plan.why: Why a proxy, not a larger database? The proxy shares a few database connections among many short function connections, so the database keeps its size; the proxy has [an hourly rate for proxies] of its own (lambda-rds-proxy-hourly-charge).
plan.exam_signal: "too many connections errors when the functions scale" points to RDS Proxy (rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling); "remove the database password from the function code" points to the proxy with the function's [IAM execution role] (rds-proxy-faq-lambda-iam-execution-role).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: put RDS Proxy between the functions and the database, so that connections are pooled. The thing to watch is the extra hourly charge.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team adds RDS Proxy and wants a reporting tool outside AWS to connect to the proxy over the internet. Can it? Answer: no; [The proxy can't be publicly accessible] (rds-proxy-same-vpc-not-public). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: A function URL is the simplest HTTPS endpoint and API Gateway adds API features

plan.problem: A team needs an HTTPS endpoint for one function. Partners will call it, and some partners need their own request limits.
trace: **Function URL.** A function URL is [public (no authentication)] or can [require IAM authentication] (lambda-furl-auth-public-or-iam); with auth type NONE the resource-based policy [must grant public access] (lambda-function-url-auth-types), or callers get [403 Forbidden] (lambda-function-url-403-without-policy).

**What it lacks.** It has [built-in cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) support] but [don't offer request transformation or validation] (lambda-furl-cors-no-validation). Rephrase so that the verbatim display fits the sentence.

**API Gateway.** API Gateway [invokes your function synchronously] (lambda-apigateway-sync-proxy-event) and adds [API keys for usage plans] and [WAF integration for additional security] (lambda-apigw-extra-features-waf-keys).

**Load balancer.** An Application Load Balancer can use [Lambda functions as a target] and route to them [based on path or header values] (lambda-alb-target-rules-sync); only an ALB has this target type (elb-lambda-target-alb-only; chapter 14, xref).
plan.table: Function URL or API Gateway (columns: Question | Function URL | API Gateway): recommended for | [simple applications or prototyping] (lambda-furl-recommended-simple-apps) | [production applications at scale] (lambda-apigw-better-for-production); API keys and usage plans | not offered (lambda-apigw-extra-features-waf-keys) | yes; charge for the endpoint | [no additional charges for the URL endpoint] (lambda-furl-no-endpoint-charge) | see chapter 33 (xref). No price for API Gateway: no fact here.
plan.why: Why does a function URL answer 429 instead of waiting? Nothing stands in front of the function: after the concurrency limit it returns [HTTP 429 responses], and [There's no built-in queuing mechanism] (lambda-furl-429-no-queue).
plan.exam_signal: "each partner needs its own API key and request quota" points to API Gateway with usage plans (lambda-apigw-extra-features-waf-keys); "the quickest HTTPS endpoint for one function, signed with IAM credentials" points to a function URL with auth type [AWS_IAM] (lambda-function-url-auth-types).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a function URL gives one function an HTTPS address, and API Gateway adds keys, limits and WAF. The thing to watch is that a URL has no queue.
plan.stop_and_answer: A function attached to a VPC must stream a large report to browsers through its function URL. Does streaming work? Answer: no; function URLs [do not support response streaming] within a VPC (lambda-streaming-furl-not-in-vpc). Keep this fact out of the trace. Lambda@Edge belongs to chapter 15: at most an xref.

sections.heading: Short event-driven work fits Lambda and long or steady work fits containers or instances
sections.diagram: lambda-compute-ladder, after the table (its alt and caption count toward this subsection: keep the alt at about 40 words)

plan.problem: A company runs three kinds of work: a thumbnail after each upload, an API that is busy all day, and video jobs that run for most of an hour. One compute service does not fit all three.
trace: **Price.** Lambda charges for the [number of requests served] and for duration [measured in GB-seconds] (lambda-pricing-dimensions); you do not [pay for idle capacity] (lambda-no-pay-for-idle-capacity).

**Short and bursty.** AWS suggests functions for [event-driven tasks, unpredictable workloads] (lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable), and you typically [pay less with Lambda at lower traffic volumes] (lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume).
**Long.** A function runs [15 minutes per invocation], while Fargate has [no hard limit on execution time] (lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit).

**Steady.** For [sustained, high-throughput workloads], Fargate's per-second billing tends to cost less (lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume), and Lambda Managed Instances suit work that is [steady-state or predictable] (lambda-choose-managed-instances-steady-state).
plan.table: Which compute for which work (columns: Work | Fits | Because): a thumbnail after each upload | a Lambda function | [event-driven tasks, unpredictable workloads] (lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable); an API busy all day | Fargate, or Lambda Managed Instances | [sustained, high-throughput workloads] (lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume); video jobs longer than the function timeout | Fargate, AWS Batch or EC2 | [no hard limit on execution time] (lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit); Batch [automatically provisions compute resources] (ec2-neighbour-batch-provisions-for-jobs). Write job lengths in words, not as a number with a unit, unless a link carries it.
plan.why: Why does steady load favor containers? Fargate is [billed per second, with a one-minute minimum charge] for what you provision, while Lambda bills the [number of requests and execution duration] (lambda-vs-fargate-billing): a busy container uses what it pays for, and at a high, steady volume the per-request bill grows past it.
plan.exam_signal: "runs for a few seconds after each upload" or "unpredictable traffic" with "LEAST operational overhead" points to Lambda (lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable); "one commitment that lowers the cost of Lambda, Fargate and EC2" points to a Compute Savings Plan, which covers [AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda usage] (lambda-compute-savings-plans-apply).
plan.body_extras: One sentence, only if words remain: Lambda also has [Durable Functions that can run up to one year] (lambda-two-programming-models), cost-effective for workflows that [spend most of their time waiting] (lambda-durable-vs-fargate-wait-heavy); chapter 32 compares them with Step Functions (xref). Lambda Managed Instances add a [15% management fee] on the EC2 price (lambda-managed-instances-fee-and-ec2-discounts).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Lambda for short work that comes in bursts, containers or instances for long or steady work. The thing to watch is how long one run takes.
plan.stop_and_answer: The company already has an EC2 Instance Savings Plan. Does it lower the bill of its busy functions? Answer: no; for Lambda only [Compute Savings Plans] apply (lambda-sp-ec2-instance-plans-exclude-lambda). Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: FAQ quick-fire
sections.plan: Ten 'FAQ <n>.' prompts (see faq), each answered in one clause in its reveal and followed by an AWS quote block of whole sentences from the fact's evidence quote (all ten facts quote https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/faqs/). At most 450 words. A quote block may say 'we' (AWS text, exempt); a link text never uses a 'we' display.

traps.belief: If a job needs more than 15 minutes, you can raise the function timeout with a Service Quotas request.
traps.truth: The maximum timeout is 900 seconds (15 minutes), and function configuration quotas such as the timeout cannot be changed. Longer work moves to AWS Fargate, AWS Batch or EC2, or is split into steps.

traps.belief: Reserved concurrency keeps environments warm, so it removes cold starts.
traps.truth: Reserved concurrency only sets aside part of the account pool for one function and caps it there, at no extra charge. Provisioned concurrency keeps pre-initialized environments ready, and you pay for it while it is configured.

traps.belief: Lambda scales without limit, so a sudden spike never gets throttled.
traps.truth: All functions of an account in a Region share one concurrency quota (1,000 by default), each function adds environments at a fixed rate, and requests beyond the limit fail with a 429 throttling error.

traps.belief: A function attached to a public subnet of a VPC reaches the internet through the internet gateway.
traps.truth: Connecting a function to a public subnet gives it no internet access and no public IP address. Attach it to private subnets whose route goes through a NAT gateway.

traps.belief: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan or Reserved Instances also lower the cost of Lambda functions.
traps.truth: Only Compute Savings Plans apply to Lambda usage; EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Reserved Instances do not.

traps.belief: A function can keep user sessions or job state in memory or in /tmp between invocations.
traps.truth: Memory and /tmp belong to one execution environment and survive only while Lambda reuses that environment; concurrent requests run in other environments, and Lambda recycles environments every few hours. State that must last goes to a durable store such as DynamoDB or Amazon S3.

traps.belief: Lambda retries every failed invocation by itself, also when API Gateway or an SDK call waits for the answer.
traps.truth: Lambda retries asynchronous invocations (two more times by default). A synchronous invocation returns the error to the caller, which must retry; the CLI and SDKs retry only client timeouts, throttling and service errors.

traps.belief: For an SQS event source, the function's dead-letter queue or on-failure destination catches the messages that keep failing.
traps.truth: For a queue source, the source queue's visibility timeout and redrive policy decide the retries and where failed messages go: give the source queue a dead-letter queue with a maxReceiveCount of at least 5. The function's dead-letter queue and destinations serve asynchronous invocations.

traps.belief: A concurrency quota increase in the primary Region also applies in the standby Region.
traps.truth: Lambda quotas for concurrency apply per AWS Region. Request the same increase in the standby Region before a failover, and check that no quota was changed in one Region but not in the other; quotas do not rise by themselves when you need them.

traps.belief: You turn on provisioned concurrency for the function as a whole, and every caller gets the warm environments.
traps.truth: Provisioned concurrency applies to a published version or an alias, not to $LATEST, and an event source must call that version or alias, or it does not use the provisioned environments.

traps.belief: To give a function more CPU, you choose a CPU setting, as you choose an instance type.
traps.truth: Memory is the setting: Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to the memory you choose, up to 6 vCPU. Raising memory can fix a compute or network bottleneck.

traps.belief: Each invocation can open and close its own database connection, because the database scales with Lambda.
traps.truth: Amazon RDS has fixed capacity, and many concurrent environments can exhaust its connection limit. Use RDS Proxy to pool connections, and open a connection in the initialization code so that warm invocations reuse it.

traps.belief: A function URL gives each client its own API key, request quota and AWS WAF protection, like API Gateway.
traps.truth: A function URL is public or uses IAM authentication, has CORS support and puts no queue in front of the function. API keys for usage plans and AWS WAF integration are features that API Gateway adds and function URLs lack.

traps.belief: Provisioned concurrency sets the largest number of copies that a function can run.
traps.truth: Provisioned concurrency is a number of pre-initialized environments, and Lambda can scale the function above and beyond that setting. Reserved concurrency is the setting that caps one function.

traps.belief: A function's dead-letter queue keeps the error details of each failed asynchronous event.
traps.truth: Lambda sends a dead-letter queue only the content of the event, without details about the response. An on-failure destination receives an invocation record with the details.

traps.belief: For a Kinesis event source, the function's dead-letter queue catches the records that keep failing.
traps.truth: A function's dead-letter queue serves asynchronous invocations. A Kinesis event source mapping retries a failed batch until the record expires by default, and it keeps discarded records only in an on-failure destination of the mapping.

traps.belief: AWS raises a Lambda concurrency quota by itself when a workload reaches it.
traps.truth: A quota rises when you request and track an increase in Service Quotas, in each Region. Assuming that quotas rise automatically is a Well-Architected anti-pattern, so request the increase before the load arrives.

traps.belief: A function's dead-letter queue also keeps the events of failed synchronous invocations.
traps.truth: A dead-letter queue or a failed-event destination receives asynchronous events after Lambda's retries. A synchronous invocation returns its error to the caller, which retries and keeps the failed request itself.

traps.belief: Lambda layers add room beyond the size quota of the deployment package.
traps.truth: The unzipped function and all its layers together stay within 250 MB. Larger dependencies go into a container image of up to 10 GB.

faq.q: Does Lambda have maintenance windows that stop my functions?
faq.answer: No; it has no maintenance windows or scheduled downtimes

faq.q: Does a function stay available while you update its code?
faq.answer: Yes; for a brief window either version can answer

faq.answer: Not as such, but a default safety throttle applies per account and Region

faq.answer: Amazon S3 can keep and retry them for a day

faq.answer: An SQS queue or an SNS topic

faq.answer: The function's role or the queue's policy; the more restrictive one wins

question_slots.note: Users upload photos to an S3 bucket at sporadic times; each photo needs a thumbnail, which takes a few seconds. LEAST operational overhead. Key: an S3 event notification that invokes a Lambda function (lambda-trigger-s3-async, lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable). Distractors: a cron job on an EC2 instance that lists the bucket every minute (works, but more effort: trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-works-means-correct; its why can cite lambda-eda-polling-inefficient); an always-on container service that polls the bucket (misconception: pays for idle capacity, lambda-no-pay-for-idle-capacity); an Auto Scaling group of instances behind a load balancer that receives the uploads (violates-qualifier).

question_slots.note: Shared stem: a company receives video files in an S3 bucket at unpredictable times; it wants to avoid managing servers and pays only while files are processed. Changed phrase: 'Each file takes about 30 seconds to process.' Key: (A) a Lambda function that an S3 event notification invokes (lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable, lambda-best-suited-short-invocations). Options identical in q09, in neutral words: (A) a Lambda function invoked for each new file; (B) containers on AWS Fargate, started for each new file; (C) an EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of one instance that checks the bucket for new files; (D) a Lambda function with its timeout raised above 15 minutes through a Service Quotas request (trap lambda-trap-timeout-raisable; impossible-feature, its why links lambda-config-quotas-not-changeable). In q02, option B fails the 'pays only while processed' and overhead comparison (misconception: lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume).

A function that compresses images is CPU-bound and too slow at its current memory setting. LEAST development effort. Key: increase the function's memory (lambda-cpu-proportional-to-memory, lambda-memory-tuning-cpu-bound). Distractors: choose a larger vCPU setting for the function (trap lambda-trap-cpu-separate-setting; impossible-feature); raise the timeout (misconception: it lets the run last longer but does not make it faster); configure provisioned concurrency (misconception: it removes initialization latency, not compute time, lambda-faq-pc-what).

During monthly campaigns, an API (API Gateway with Lambda) returns TooManyRequestsException; CloudWatch shows that the total concurrency of all functions in the Region reaches the account quota. Ensure that all requests are served during the next campaign. Key: request a higher concurrent executions quota for the Region in Service Quotas (lambda-faq-limit-increase-service-quotas, lambda-concurrent-executions-default, lambda-throttle-429). Distractors: nothing to change, because Lambda scales without limit and the error is transient (trap lambda-trap-scales-without-limit); raise the memory of the functions (misconception); configure provisioned concurrency on every function (misconception: provisioned concurrency counts toward the account limit, lambda-provisioned-concurrency-charges). Do not key on the number 1,000.

A company runs its serverless application in one Region and keeps a standby copy in a second Region for disaster recovery. Last year it raised the Lambda concurrency quota in the primary Region. In a failover test, the functions in the standby Region are throttled. Ensure the standby can carry the full load. Key: request the same concurrency quota increase in the standby Region ahead of time, and check quotas in both Regions automatically (lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc, lambda-wa-quotas-failover-region). Distractors: nothing to do, because the increase applies in every Region of the account (trap lambda-trap-quota-follows-region); wait for AWS to raise the quota automatically during the failover (misconception: lambda-wa-quotas-not-auto-increased names it an anti-pattern); set reserved concurrency for the functions in the standby Region (misconception: reservations divide the Regional quota, they do not raise it, lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control).

question_slots.twin: first of strict twin pair B (twin q13)
question_slots.note: Shared stem: an API on API Gateway invokes a Lambda function that writes to a small relational database. Changed phrase: 'During spikes, so many copies of the function connect that the database fails; the function must never run more than 50 copies at the same time.' Key: (A) set the function's reserved concurrency to 50 (lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control, lambda-bp-reserved-protects-downstream). Options identical in q13: (A) set reserved concurrency to 50; (B) configure provisioned concurrency on an alias that API Gateway invokes; (C) raise the function's memory to the maximum; (D) turn on SnapStart together with provisioned concurrency (impossible-feature: lambda-faq-snapstart-pc-exclusive). In q06, option B fails because provisioned concurrency is no ceiling: Lambda scales [above and beyond your provisioned concurrency setting] (lambda-pc-scales-beyond-setting) (misconception).

An order service calls a Lambda function synchronously with the AWS SDK and does not need the result at once. Sometimes the function fails because a downstream system is briefly unavailable, and those orders are lost. Ensure that failed orders are retried and kept for review without changing the downstream system. Key: invoke the function asynchronously and configure an on-failure destination, such as an SQS queue (lambda-async-default-two-retries, lambda-async-discard-then-destination, lambda-async-destination-targets). Distractors: rely on Lambda's automatic retries of synchronous invocations (trap lambda-trap-lambda-retries-sync); raise the function timeout (misconception); configure a dead-letter queue on the function and keep the synchronous call (misconception: the dead-letter queue serves asynchronous invocations, lambda-faq-dlq-after-retries).

Amazon S3 invokes a function for each upload. Some uploads fail every attempt. The team must keep each failed event with its error details, and must see it within minutes instead of after hours of retries. Select TWO. Keys: configure an on-failure destination that is a standard SQS queue (lambda-async-destination-targets, lambda-dlq-content-only-vs-destinations: a destination keeps details, a dead-letter queue keeps only the content); lower the maximum retry attempts and the maximum event age in the asynchronous configuration (lambda-async-retry-attempts-0-to-2, lambda-async-max-event-age-6-hours). Distractors: a dead-letter queue on the function (violates-requirement: [only sends the content of the event]); an Amazon SNS FIFO topic as the destination (impossible-feature: lambda-destination-fifo-unsupported); an S3 bucket as the on-success destination for later analysis (impossible-feature: lambda-async-s3-destination-on-failure-only). Keep at most one impossible-feature distractor in the final five options: replace one with a misconception, for example 'turn on S3 Versioning to keep the failed events'.

An SQS queue decouples an order service from a Lambda function that an event source mapping invokes. A few malformed messages fail again and again and fill the logs; the team wants to keep them for later analysis. LEAST operational overhead. Key: give the source queue a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue and a maxReceiveCount of at least 5 (lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue, lambda-sqs-dlq-maxreceivecount-5). Distractors: configure a dead-letter queue or an on-failure destination on the function (trap lambda-trap-function-dlq-for-sqs); set the queue's visibility timeout lower than the function timeout so that failures return sooner (impossible-feature: lambda-sqs-timeout-not-above-visibility); have the function delete any message it cannot parse (violates-requirement: the messages are not kept).

A function must query an RDS database in private subnets and must call a payment provider's API on the internet. MOST secure. Key: attach the function to private subnets whose route table sends internet traffic to a NAT gateway in a public subnet (lambda-vpc-public-subnet-no-internet, lambda-vpc-attach-private-subnets). Distractors: attach the function to public subnets so that it uses the internet gateway (trap lambda-trap-public-subnet-internet); leave the function outside the VPC and make the database publicly accessible (violates-qualifier); associate an Elastic IP address with the function (impossible-feature; no Lambda fact says it, so the why says the function's network interface is created by Lambda: lambda-hyperplane-eni-shared-by-subnet-sg).

Functions behind API Gateway write orders to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. In traffic spikes, the database returns 'too many connections' errors. Every request must be served; LEAST operational overhead; minimal code changes. Key: create an RDS Proxy and point the functions at the proxy endpoint (lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy, rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling, rds-proxy-faq-no-code-changes). Wrong path in the think-aloud: the first idea, 'set reserved concurrency to cap the copies', breaks because capped requests are throttled with a [throttling error (429 status code)] (lambda-throttle-429), and every request must be served. Distractors: open and close a connection in each invocation (trap lambda-trap-connection-per-invocation); reserved concurrency of 10 (violates-requirement); a larger database instance class (violates-qualifier: more cost and a resize, and connections still grow with concurrency).

Changed phrase: 'After quiet periods, the first requests take several seconds; the API must answer within double-digit milliseconds every time.' Key: (B) provisioned concurrency on an alias that API Gateway invokes (lambda-faq-pc-what, lambda-pc-not-latest-no-cold-start, lambda-pc-event-source-alias). Same four options as q06; option A carries trap lambda-trap-reserved-keeps-warm; option C fails (misconception: memory does not remove initialization); option D is impossible (lambda-faq-snapstart-pc-exclusive).

A team configured provisioned concurrency on alias 'live' of a function. However, cold starts continue: the API Gateway integration invokes the function's unqualified ARN. Key: point the integration at the alias that has provisioned concurrency (lambda-pc-event-source-alias, lambda-pc-not-latest-no-cold-start). Distractors: configure provisioned concurrency on $LATEST instead (trap lambda-trap-provisioned-on-latest; impossible-feature); add reserved concurrency to keep environments warm (trap lambda-trap-reserved-keeps-warm); raise provisioned concurrency on the alias (misconception: the unqualified ARN does not use it).

A company has steady-state usage of Lambda, Fargate and EC2 that will last three years, and it may move work between them. MOST cost-effective commitment. Key: a Compute Savings Plan (lambda-compute-savings-plans-apply, lambda-sp-ec2-instance-plans-exclude-lambda). Distractors: an EC2 Instance Savings Plan (trap lambda-trap-ec2-savings-plans-cover-lambda); Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 part and nothing for Lambda (misconception: leaves Lambda and Fargate uncovered); provisioned concurrency for every function (misconception: it adds charges, lambda-pc-costs-while-idle). Keep percentages out of the key: the two facts state different maximums (72% for all Savings Plans, 66% for Compute Savings Plans).

A containerizable API on Lambda now receives a high, steady volume of requests all day, every day; each request runs about one second at a large memory size. The company wants to lower compute cost with the least change to how it operates (no servers). Key: run the API as containers on AWS Fargate (lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume: [sustained, high-throughput workloads]; lambda-choose-fargate-containers-persistent). Distractors: add provisioned concurrency to the functions (misconception: [it increases costs], lambda-pc-costs-while-idle); raise the memory to finish each request faster (misconception: no verified fact says that the bill falls, brief.v0 d034); move the API to an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances (violates-requirement: servers to manage). Do not offer Lambda Managed Instances as an option (it would also fit, lambda-choose-managed-instances-steady-state, and makes the key ambiguous).

A function downloads the same 300 MB reference file from Amazon S3 at the start of every invocation, which makes each request slow. The file changes once a week. Select TWO. Keys: move the download into the initialization code outside the handler, so that warm invocations do not run it again (lambda-static-init-reuse-connections: [is not run again]); keep the file in /tmp and download it only when it is missing (lambda-tmp-transient-cache). Distractors: store the file in an environment variable (impossible-feature: lambda-env-vars-size, [4 KB]); download once into a global variable and never check it again, because the environment lasts forever (trap lambda-trap-state-in-environment: lambda-environment-not-persistent); raise the function timeout (misconception). The prompt number 300 MB is scenario data in the stem.

A function processes a Kinesis data stream through an event source mapping with default settings. However, one malformed record makes the function fail, and that shard stops moving for days while other shards continue. Keep the failed record for later and keep processing. Key: turn on bisect batch on function error, set a maximum retry count and a maximum record age, and add an on-failure destination (lambda-stream-bisect-batch-on-error, lambda-kinesis-bad-record-block-one-week, lambda-kinesis-on-failure-destination-targets). Distractors: configure a dead-letter queue on the function (misconception: that serves asynchronous invocations, lambda-faq-dlq-after-retries); raise the parallelization factor (misconception: records of a shard are still processed in order, lambda-ddb-stream-partition-key-order / lambda-kinesis-in-order-stops-on-error); a redrive policy on the stream (impossible-feature: a redrive policy belongs to an SQS queue, lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue).

A company exposes one Lambda function to partners over HTTPS. Each partner must use its own key and must be limited to its own request rate, and the endpoint must be protected by AWS WAF rules. LEAST operational overhead. Key: an API Gateway REST API with usage plans and API keys, with AWS WAF on the API (lambda-apigw-extra-features-waf-keys, lambda-apigw-better-for-production). Distractors: a function URL with auth type NONE and an API key check in the code (trap lambda-trap-function-url-api-features); a function URL with auth type AWS_IAM (misconception: IAM authentication gives no per-partner request limit and no WAF, lambda-furl-auth-public-or-iam); an Application Load Balancer with the function as target and a listener rule per partner (violates-qualifier: no usage plans; more to operate).

An order pipeline is a chain of Lambda functions: each calls the next one synchronously and waits for its answer, with retries written by hand. Costs are high, and nobody can see which step failed. LEAST operational overhead. Key: orchestrate the steps with AWS Step Functions, one function per task (lambda-chaining-anti-pattern-sqs-or-step-functions, lambda-step-functions-orchestrate-errors, lambda-chaining-cost-wait-state). Distractors: raise the timeouts of the calling functions so that they wait longer (misconception: they keep [running in a wait state] and are billed, lambda-chaining-cost-wait-state); merge all steps into one large function (misconception: [Hard to enforce least privilege], lambda-monolith-breaks-least-privilege); add reserved concurrency to each function (misconception). Do not offer durable functions as an option (also a valid design in the guide, lambda-durable-vs-step-functions-focus): the key would be ambiguous. Chapter 32 owns Step Functions; this question tests only that chaining is the anti-pattern.

A function needs machine learning libraries that are larger than the .zip deployment package quota when unzipped. The company wants to keep using Lambda. Which combination of steps meets the requirement? (Select TWO.) Keys: build the function as a container image that includes the libraries (lambda-container-image-10-gb, lambda-faq-deploy-zip-or-image); store the image in Amazon ECR in the same Region as the function (lambda-container-image-ecr-same-region). Distractors: split the libraries into five layers (misconception: the function and its layers together stay within [250 MB], lambda-layers-five-and-250-mb); upload the .zip archive through Amazon S3 instead of directly (misconception: the unzipped limit of [250 MB] still applies, lambda-package-250-mb-unzipped); store the image in an ECR repository in another Region (impossible-feature: lambda-container-image-ecr-same-region). Do not offer 'download the libraries into /tmp at start-up': it can also work, and the key would be ambiguous.

A nightly batch job invokes thousands of functions at once and uses the whole account pool; at that time the mission-critical payment function is throttled. Ensure the payment function can always scale to its usual peak. Key: configure reserved concurrency for the payment function (lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control, lambda-reserved-concurrency-no-charge). Distractors: nothing to change, because every function scales on demand without limit (trap lambda-trap-scales-without-limit); provisioned concurrency on the batch function (misconception); a larger memory setting for the payment function (misconception).
