tasks.title: Read your Lambda concurrency quota in two Regions
tasks.kills: "Lambda scales without limit, in every Region the same."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, read-only, 3 minutes, $0. Step 1: aws lambda get-account-settings --query AccountLimit (expect ConcurrentExecutions and UnreservedConcurrentExecutions; the default is [1,000] (lambda-concurrent-executions-default), and a new account can show less, because new accounts have [reduced concurrency and memory quotas] (lambda-new-account-reduced-quotas)). Step 2: the same command with --region us-west-2 (expect its own numbers: quotas apply [per AWS Region], lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc). Step 3: aws service-quotas list-service-quotas --service-code lambda --query 'Quotas[].[QuotaName,Value,Adjustable]' --output table (expect some quotas with Adjustable true and some false: [hard limits, which you cannot change] and [soft limits, which you can request increases for], lambda-quotas-hard-vs-soft). Creates nothing. Commands from official CLI pages in the corpus (tasks check-cli --reference). The expect texts state no AWS number except through these facts.

tasks.title: Stop a function with reserved concurrency zero and start it again
tasks.kills: "A function always scales to meet its requests."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, about 10 minutes. Create role saa-lambda-t02 with aws iam create-role and an inline trust policy for [lambda.amazonaws.com] (lambda-execution-role-trust-lambda-principal), tagged book=saa and task=lambda-t02; attach the AWS managed policy [AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole] (lambda-execution-role-required-logs); aws iam wait role-exists. Create function saa-lambda-t02 (a Python runtime, a handler that returns a short JSON body), tagged book=saa and task=lambda-t02; aws lambda wait function-active-v2. Function code in one plain command: the writer chooses what tasks check-cli accepts, either aws lambda create-function with --code ZipFile=<base64 of a small zip> (CLI v2 reads blobs as base64; the step text names the value), or aws cloudformation create-stack --template-body with an inline Python ZipFile handler (then the cleanup is delete-stack); no redirect, no local file. Invoke synchronously: expect StatusCode 200. Break it: predict, then aws lambda put-function-concurrency --reserved-concurrent-executions 0; invoke again: expect a TooManyRequestsException (Rate Exceeded), because reserved concurrency 0 stops all invocations ([set its reserved concurrency to 0], lambda-reserved-concurrency-zero-throttles; [429 error code], lambda-faq-throttle-sync-429). Fix: aws lambda delete-function-concurrency; invoke: expect 200. Cleanup: delete-function, detach-role-policy, delete-role (in reverse order of creation). Verify by name (TOOLS-rules R6): aws lambda get-function --function-name saa-lambda-t02, expect ResourceNotFoundException. Cost line: '$0' only with a fact: a few invocations within the free tier ([one million requests], lambda-free-tier); cost_if_forgotten '$0', because a function costs nothing while idle ([pay for idle capacity], lambda-no-pay-for-idle-capacity); if T109 or the reviewers refuse the free-tier claim, state the cost with lambda-price-per-million-requests and lambda-price-per-gb-second as cost_facts. Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'. No IAM user, no access key.

tasks.title: Invoke a failing function both ways and find each error
tasks.kills: "Lambda retries every failed invocation and keeps the failed event."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, about 15 minutes. Create queue saa-lambda-t03-failed (aws sqs create-queue with tags book=saa and task=lambda-t03); capture its ARN with aws sqs get-queue-attributes. Create role saa-lambda-t03 (trust policy for lambda.amazonaws.com, tags), attach AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole, and add an inline policy (put-role-policy) that allows sqs:SendMessage on that queue ARN only. Create function saa-lambda-t03 whose handler raises an error (same code approach as lambda-t02), tagged. Set the asynchronous configuration: aws lambda put-function-event-invoke-config --maximum-retry-attempts 0 --destination-config OnFailure={Destination=$QUEUE_ARN} (retries can be set [between 0 and 2], lambda-async-retry-attempts-0-to-2). Step: invoke synchronously: expect StatusCode 200 and FunctionError Unhandled, because the [status code is 200, even if the function returned an error] (lambda-sync-status-200-with-function-error). Break it: predict 'Is this failed synchronous call now in the queue?', then aws sqs receive-message on the queue: expect no messages, because the caller must [retry the invocation manually] (lambda-sync-error-caller-retries). Then invoke with --invocation-type Event: expect StatusCode 202, because Lambda [returns a success response] after it [places the event in a queue] (lambda-async-queue-then-separate-process). Receive from the queue again after a short wait: expect one record with the error, because without retries left [Lambda discards it] unless you [configure a failed-event destination] (lambda-async-discard-then-destination). Cleanup in reverse order: delete-function-event-invoke-config, delete-function, delete-role-policy, detach-role-policy, delete-role, delete-queue. Verify by name: aws lambda get-function --function-name saa-lambda-t03, expect ResourceNotFoundException. Cost line as lambda-t02 (SQS requests: no price fact here; keep '$0' only if a free-tier fact covers it, else name the facts). Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'.

speak.prompt: Why not move the audio conversion to Lambda too, and delete the workers?
speak.note: Short answer: keep the long conversions on the workers; a function stops at fifteen minutes, and our longest recording takes twenty-five minutes to convert. How it works: Lambda fits short jobs that start on an event; long or heavy work runs on instances or containers, which have no such limit. Watch: steady heavy work also tends to cost less on instances or containers than on functions. In your case: 'Could we split long recordings into parts that each convert in a few minutes?' Must not say: 'Lambda has no GPU' (no AWS page says it, brief.v0 d115); 'we can raise the timeout'; 'Lambda is always cheaper'. Numbers as words, from the spoken forms of the fact cards (fifteen minutes: lambda-faq-timeout-15-minutes or lambda-timeout-max).

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Reserved concurrency or provisioned concurrency: which one fixes our slow first requests?
speak.note: First sentence may start 'Both'. Short answer: provisioned concurrency; reserved concurrency only sets aside and caps capacity, and it warms nothing. How it works: provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized on a version or an alias, so the first requests skip the cold start. Watch: you pay for those environments all day; scale them on a schedule with Application Auto Scaling. In your case: 'When do your slow requests happen: after quiet nights, or at a known time each morning?' Must not say: 'reserved concurrency keeps functions warm'; 'provisioned concurrency is free'; 'turn it on for $LATEST'.

speak.prompt: Our Lambda functions take down our PostgreSQL database during traffic spikes. What do we change?
speak.note: Short answer: put Amazon RDS Proxy between the functions and the database. How it works: each copy of a function opens its own connection, and the database has a fixed limit; the proxy pools and shares a smaller number of database connections and queues the rest in a surge. Watch: open the connection outside the handler so warm copies reuse it, and remember the proxy has its own hourly charge. In your case: 'Must every request be served, or can some wait or be rejected at the peak?' (if some can be rejected, reserved concurrency also caps the copies). Must not say: 'buy a bigger database and the problem goes away'; 'open and close a connection in every request'.

speak.prompt: If no calls arrive at night, do we still pay for the functions?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain 'function' as 'a small piece of our code that AWS runs when work arrives' the first time. Short answer: no; we pay for each run and how long it takes, so a quiet night costs almost nothing. How it works: AWS starts the code when an upload arrives and stops charging when it ends; there is no machine waiting for us. Watch: if we ever pay to keep functions warm for speed, that part costs money even at night. In your case: 'Is morning speed worth a small fixed cost, or is a short delay on the first upload fine?' Must not say: 'it is free' (other services such as the queue or the database still cost money); 'we pay nothing at all'.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, a job runs for most of an hour after each upload, with no servers to manage. Function or Fargate?
cards.back: AWS Fargate. A function stops after 15 minutes per invocation.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, reserved or provisioned concurrency: which one removes cold starts?
cards.back: Provisioned concurrency.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, a CPU-heavy function is slow. Which setting do you raise?
cards.back: Memory. CPU grows in proportion to it.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, does Lambda retry a failed synchronous invocation by itself?
cards.back: No. The caller retries.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, a function in a VPC must call an internet API. What does it need?
cards.back: Private subnets with a route to a NAT gateway.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, many concurrent functions exhaust the connections of an RDS database. What do you add?
cards.back: Amazon RDS Proxy.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, the maximum timeout of a function is {{c1::900 seconds}}.
In AWS Lambda, the default timeout of a new function is {{c1::3 seconds}}.
In AWS Lambda, a function's memory can be set from 128 MB to {{c1::10,240 MB}}.
In AWS Lambda, the default concurrent executions quota per account per Region is {{c1::1,000}}.
In AWS Lambda, after a failed asynchronous invocation, Lambda by default tries {{c1::two more times}}.
In AWS Lambda, a synchronous request payload can be at most {{c1::6 MB}}.
In AWS Lambda, a container image function can be up to {{c1::10 GB}} uncompressed.
In AWS Lambda, the /tmp storage of a function can be set from 512 MB to {{c1::10,240 MB}}.
In AWS Lambda, can a Service Quotas request raise the maximum function timeout?
cards.back: No. Function configuration quotas cannot be changed.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda with an SQS event source, where do the messages that keep failing go?
cards.back: To the source queue's dead-letter queue, through its redrive policy.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda with an SQS event source, how long should the queue's visibility timeout be?
cards.back: At least six times the function timeout.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, a standby Region must take the full load after a failover. Which quota do you raise there?
cards.back: That Region's concurrency quota, ahead of time.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, can you configure provisioned concurrency on $LATEST?
cards.back: No. Only on a published version or an alias.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, SnapStart or provisioned concurrency: which one fits a strict double-digit millisecond startup?
cards.back: Provisioned concurrency. SnapStart is best effort.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, partners need their own API keys and usage plans. Function URL or API Gateway?
cards.back: Amazon API Gateway.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, which kind of Savings Plan lowers the cost of functions?
cards.back: A Compute Savings Plan.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, where does data go that must survive between invocations?
cards.back: A durable store, such as DynamoDB or Amazon S3.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, how do you stop a runaway function at once without deleting it?
cards.back: Set its reserved concurrency to 0.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, an event source mapping can deliver one record twice. How must the code behave?
cards.back: Idempotently: a repeated record changes nothing.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, can an S3 bucket be the on-success destination of asynchronous invocations?
cards.back: No. An S3 bucket serves on failure only.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda with an SQS event source, how do you retry only the failed messages of a batch?
cards.back: A partial batch response (ReportBatchItemFailures).

cards.front: In AWS Lambda with a Kinesis stream, one bad record blocks a shard. Which setting splits the failed batch?
cards.back: BisectBatchOnFunctionError.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, trigger or event source mapping: which one is a resource of the Lambda service?
cards.back: The event source mapping.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, Amazon S3 must invoke a function. Which policy must allow it?
cards.back: The function's resource-based policy.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, how do you send a small share of traffic to a new version?
cards.back: A weighted alias, as a canary release.

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, where does AWS recommend keeping database credentials?
cards.back: AWS Secrets Manager, not environment variables.

diagrams.title: One event through AWS Lambda
diagrams.claim: Each request runs in a free execution environment, and Lambda creates a new one when none is free.
diagrams.alt: A sequence with four participants: an event source, the Lambda service, a warm execution environment and a new execution environment. Two events arrive together. The first goes to the warm environment; for the second, Lambda starts a new environment and runs its initialization first.
say: An event source invokes the function, or Lambda polls a queue and gets a batch.
Lambda sends the request to a free execution environment of the function, if a warm one is free.
When no environment is free, Lambda downloads the code and starts a new environment: a cold start.
The handler processes the event with the permissions of the function's execution role.
Each environment handles one request at a time, so two requests at once need two environments.
diagrams.note: Size s. Participants: event source (generic icon or the s3 icon), Lambda service (lambda icon), environment A (warm), environment B (new, emph). Steps 1 to 5 as numbered messages. In the Markdown steps link step 1 to lambda-event-push-or-pull ([direct invocation (push)] or [event source mappings (pull)]), step 2 to lambda-warm-start-environment-reuse ([Lambda can reuse the environment]), step 3 to lambda-cold-start-definition ([downloads your code, starts the environment]), step 4 to lambda-faq-execution-role ([IAM role]) and step 5 to lambda-managed-instances-multi-concurrency-row ([a maximum of one invocation at a time]). Rephrase a step only so that the verbatim display fits; keep spec say and Markdown steps equal (L703). No AWS number in labels or steps.

diagrams.title: Three ways to invoke a function
diagrams.claim: A synchronous caller waits for the answer, an asynchronous event waits in Lambda's queue, and an event source mapping polls for batches.
diagrams.alt: Three panels. In the first, API Gateway calls the function and waits for the response. In the second, Amazon S3 hands an event to Lambda's internal queue and gets a success response at once. In the third, Lambda polls an SQS queue and invokes the function with a batch.
panels: Synchronous: API Gateway (apigateway) -> function (lambda) 'request'; function -> API Gateway 'response'
Asynchronous: Amazon S3 (s3) -> event queue (lambda) 'event'; event queue -> function 'retries' (emph)
Event source mapping: Lambda poller (lambda) -> SQS queue (sqs) 'poll'; poller -> function 'batch'
diagrams.note: Size m, three panels with the same structure (source left, Lambda middle, function right), at most 3 nodes and 2 edges each; edge labels at most 3 words; no numbers. The caption (the claim) links [runs the function and waits for a response] (lambda-sync-invocation-waits), [places the event in a queue] (lambda-async-queue-then-separate-process) and [Lambda handles the polling] (lambda-esm-lambda-polls-source); rephrase the caption so that each display stands verbatim, and keep the spec claim equal to it (L702). Caption at most 24 words.

diagrams.title: Which compute for this work?
diagrams.claim: How long one run lasts and how steady the load is decide between a function, a container and an instance.
diagrams.alt: A decision ladder with three questions. Work that starts on an event and ends within minutes leads to a Lambda function; long or steady container work leads to AWS Fargate; work that needs control of the host leads to Amazon EC2.
rungs: Does each run start on an event and end within minutes? -> Lambda function (icon lambda, emph)
Is it long or steady container work? -> AWS Fargate (icon fargate)
Do you need control of the host? -> Amazon EC2 (icon ec2)
diagrams.note: Ladder kind: questions at most 9 words, outcomes at most 4 words; no numbers with units in labels. AWS Batch is not a rung (one clause in the table). The caption links [short-lived, event-driven tasks] (lambda-fargate-long-running-lambda-short) or the decision-guide display; keep the spec claim equal to the caption.

diagrams.title: Callvale before: scheduled jobs on the worker
diagrams.claim: One worker instance runs the conversions and the small scheduled jobs, so a busy worker stops them all.
diagrams.alt: Before: the web tier sends each upload to the one worker instance and waits. On the worker, scheduled jobs register uploads, save results and send notifications. The worker writes job status to the PostgreSQL database. The worker is marked as overloaded.
say: The web tier sends each upload to the one worker instance.
Scheduled jobs on the worker register uploads, save results and send notifications.
On launch day the conversions fill the worker, and the small jobs stop too.
diagrams.note: Story picture (pipeline state P1 of STARTUP B1). Steps are story, not AWS rules: no fact link, no number (the 6 hours and 900 connections stay in the Context text). Keep each component in the same grid cell as in lambda-after (STARTUP A7 rule 13): users and the web tier on the left, compute in the middle, the database on the right, integration under compute.

diagrams.title: Callvale after: functions that events invoke
diagrams.claim: Events now start small functions, while the long conversions stay on the workers and the database is reached through RDS Proxy.
diagrams.alt: After: an upload to the audio bucket sends an event to the uploads queue. The start-job function polls it and puts work on the convert queue for the conversion workers. The save-results and notify functions finish each job; save-results reaches PostgreSQL through RDS Proxy.
say: An upload to the audio bucket sends an event to the uploads queue.
The start-job function reads the uploads queue through an event source mapping.
Start-job puts the conversion on the convert queue, and the workers convert the audio.
The save-results function stores the results through RDS Proxy.
